sens: Bring back to a previous state, to health
Restore an order, a political or spiritual situation
Give back, return
G0600.detail:
1. Restore someone to their health or physical integrity: when Jesus heals the withered hand of the man, it "became" healthy (Matthew 12:13), or when he gives sight to the blind man who "was healed" (Mark 8:25). The word evokes a return to normalcy, as if putting back in place what was damaged.

2. Restore the order of things, particularly the divine order of the world or of the people: Elijah must come to "restore all things" (Matthew 17:11), and the apostles ask if Jesus will "restore the kingdom of Israel" (Acts 1:6). It is a renewal of God's plan, a spiritual and political reordering.

3. Give back or return to someone what belongs to them: the apostle Paul asks that his friend Timothy be "returned" to him (Hebrews 13:19), meaning that he should be brought back to him. The word here implies a return to the one who is waiting.
G0600.origine: The Greek word is composed of a preposition "apo" (from, again) and a form of the verb "kathistēmi" (establish, place, institute). Together, they evoke the idea of "placing back in order," of "restoring." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew "shub" (to return), which emphasizes the movement of restoration and return to a previous state.
G0600.emploi: The verb appears about 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Matthew and Mark. In the Gospels, it primarily describes miraculous healings: when Jesus restores the health of a sick person or a blind man, he demonstrates his power of restoration. In messianic sayings (Matthew 17:11, Mark 9:12, Acts 1:6), the word takes on an eschatological significance: it refers to the renewal of all things that God will accomplish at the end of time. In Hebrews 13:19, the meaning is restricted to the simple restitution or return of a loved one.
G0600.portee: This word reveals the mission of Jesus: he does not come merely to condemn or destroy, but to restore, heal, and reinstate. For the believer, it is an assurance that God can bring back to order and health what was ruined or lost. It also encourages waiting with hope for the final renewal of all things promised by God.

sens: Bring to light what was hidden, discover, make visible
Show, make known a person or their identity
Make known through a divine action the truth, plan, or will of God
G0601.detail:
1. In its most common sense, the verb means to remove the veil from what was secret or unknown. It is to discover what was hidden: in Matthew 10:26, Jesus says that everything hidden "must be revealed," as if one day the curtain would be lifted on secrets. This sense also applies to Luke 2:35, where the hidden thoughts of hearts will be "revealed."

2. It also designates the appearance or manifestation of a person. In Luke 17:30, when the Son of Man "appears," the verb means that he will show himself to the eyes of all. Similarly, in 2 Thessalonians 2:3, the Antichrist must "appear," meaning he will reveal himself to the world.

3. But especially, in the Bible, this verb describes the action of God making known his truth, his hidden mysteries, and his will. When God "reveals" something, he lifts the supernatural veil on a divine secret. In Galatians 1:16, Paul says that God "revealed" his Son in him — this is not ordinary knowledge, but divine illumination. In Romans 8:18, the future glory will be "revealed," meaning that God will manifest it. It is through this divine revelation that the apostles and prophets received the Gospel and the mysteries of God's plan.
G0601.origine: The word comes from the Greek ἀπό (apo, "away from, remove") and καλύπτω (kalyptō, "cover, veil"). The basic image is therefore "remove the veil" or "take away what covers." In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb גָּלָה (galâ), which literally means "to uncover, reveal, exile." The composition of the word well expresses the movement: to take the veil far away, to remove it completely. It is a word that implies a hidden reality and an act that manifests it in the open.
G0601.emploi: This verb appears 26 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles and in the Gospels. It is first used for hidden things that must be discovered (Matthew 10:26, Luke 12:2), then for the visible appearance of Christ or the Antichrist (Luke 17:30, 2 Thessalonians 2:3-8). But its richest usage is that of divine revelation: God reveals his Son to Paul (Galatians 1:16), reveals the mysteries of the Gospel (Ephesians 3:5), shows the apostles what the Father hides from the wise (Matthew 11:25-27). It is also by revelation that the prophets came to know the Gospel of Christ (1 Peter 1:12). The word emphasizes that the knowledge of God is not acquired through human wisdom, but given by the supernatural action of God.
G0601.portee: This word reminds the reader that the greatest secrets and divine truths are not obtained through human reasoning, but through the revelation of God. It establishes trust in the apostles and prophets: what they proclaimed was shown to them by God himself. For the believer, it also means that nothing done in darkness remains hidden — God sees everything and will reveal all on the day of judgment.

sens: The act of discovering what was hidden, of bringing to light
The action of God revealing His will, His mysteries, or His plans
A divine communication given directly to a person (vision, word, illumination)
The glorious appearance of Christ at the end of times
G0602.detail: 1. In the literal sense, the word denotes the action of discovering, bringing to light what was veiled or secret (this is the starting image of the word). 2. In the Bible, it takes on a spiritual meaning: it is the action by which God removes the veil that hides His truth from men. For example, in Romans 8:19, creation awaits "the revelation of the sons of God," meaning the moment when who we are in Christ will be fully manifested. 3. The word also denotes a direct communication from God to a person in a particular form: vision, inner word, sudden illumination of the spirit. Paul speaks of this in 2 Corinthians 12:1 when he recounts "visions and revelations of the Lord," and in Galatians 1:12 when he asserts that the Gospel was delivered to him "by a revelation of Jesus Christ." 4. In the Pauline epistles, the word also takes on an eschatological dimension (concerning the last things): it denotes the glorious appearance of Christ or the children of God at the end of times (1 Thessalonians 1:7, 1 Peter 1:7).
G0602.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀποκαλύπτω (apokalyptô) which literally means "to remove the veil" (ἀπό = to take away, remove; καλύπτω = to cover, veil). It often translates the Hebrew עֶרְוָה (erva), which denotes nakedness or what is uncovered. The root always evokes the idea of removing a covering to reveal what was hidden. In biblical Greek, the word has taken on a profound theological meaning: it does not denote a mere human discovery, but an action of God that enlightens the mind of man to make known His mysteries.
G0602.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul (Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, 2 Thessalonians) and in 1 Peter and Revelation. Paul uses it to speak of the knowledge of the Gospel that he received from God alone (Galatians 1:12, Galatians 2:2, Ephesians 1:17), or to describe the mystical experiences that a believer may have (2 Corinthians 12:1). Luke uses it in 2:32 for the manifestation of Christ to the nations. In the epistles of Peter and in Revelation, the word speaks of the future appearance of Christ or the coming glory (1 Peter 1:7, 1 Peter 1:13, Revelation 1:1). The meaning varies according to the context: sometimes it refers to a past revelation (what God has shown), and sometimes to a future revelation (what God will manifest).
G0602.portee: This word invites the Christian to seek knowledge of God not in his own wisdom or human experience, but in an openness to the action of God who alone can enlighten our understanding and help us grasp His mysteries. It also reminds us that our faith rests on a real divine action: God is not distant, but active in making known the truth to us. Finally, it directs our gaze toward the future: we await the final revelation of Christ and our glory in Him, which gives meaning and hope to our present life.

sens: Intense and prolonged observation with anxiety
Passionate desire for something awaited
Mental tension directed toward a future event
G0603.detail:
1. The word paints the image of someone straining their neck, standing on tiptoe to see and watch better. It is a tense, anxious observation, that of someone waiting impatiently. In Romans 8:19, creation itself is described as waiting "with eager expectation" for the revelation of the sons of God — it scans the horizon to see that moment arrive.
2. This expectation is not passive: it is filled with emotion, with passion. It is the intense desire for a future thing that one hopes for ardently. In Philippians 1:20, Paul speaks of his "earnest expectation" and hope — he is fully focused on that moment when Christ will be glorified.
3. The word thus denotes this inner tension, this state of mind that remains fixed on a future event with intensity and hope.
G0603.origine: The Greek word is composed: "apo" (from, away) and "karadokia" (from "kara," the head, and "dokeo," to look). The primary image is that of the head raised, leaning forward, scanning the horizon — like someone craning their neck to see better. It is an energetic expression, evoking the watchman who does not take their eyes off the object of their expectation. The corresponding verb translates an ancient Greek word that expresses this tense and eager waiting (used in Psalms 37:7).
G0603.emploi: This word appears only twice in the New Testament, always in an eschatological context — that is, directed toward the future that God is preparing. In Romans 8:19, Paul uses it to describe how all creation awaits the revelation of the children of God, as if it is holding its breath, tense with expectation. In Philippians 1:20, it expresses Paul's personal expectation: he hopes firmly, eagerly, that Christ will be glorified in him. In both cases, the expectation is tense, watchful, filled with emotions and significant spiritual stakes.
G0603.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to meditate on the quality of their expectation: it is not a mere flabby hope, but a dynamic tension of heart and mind. This applies to our expectation of Christ's return, to our desire for His glory to be manifested. It is a call to not live passively, but to live in eager vigilance, in a posture of someone who cranes their neck to see their Lord arriving.

sens: Restore peace between two enemy or separated parties
Bring back to unity what was divided
Erase hostility and restore friendship
Restore a broken relationship through a complete and decisive intervention
G0604.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to restore peace between enemies: to cease enmity and restore a relationship of friendship. In Ephesians 2:16, Christ "reconciles" Jews and Gentiles into one body, destroying through the cross the hostility that separated them.

2. It denotes the action of bringing back to unity what was fragmented or divided. Reconciliation is not just individual forgiveness: it is a unification, a gathering of what was in rupture.

3. The word carries the idea of a complete and definitive restoration. The prefix "apo" (from, away) reinforced by "kata" (completely) indicates that reconciliation is total, radical, and not partial or superficial.

4. In Colossians 1:20, it is Christ who "reconciles all" — everything that exists on earth and in heaven — by bringing everything back to God through the blood of His cross. Cosmic reconciliation rests on this decisive act of Christ.
G0604.origine: The verb comes from the root "katalassō" (to exchange, to change) preceded by the prefix "apo" (completely, entirely). The basic image is that of an exchange: replacing enmity with peace, hostility with friendship. The prefix "apo" intensifies the meaning: it is not a partial or precarious reconciliation, but a total and definitive restoration. This word is infrequent in the New Testament and concentrated on the work of Christ.
G0604.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the Pauline epistles: Ephesians 2:16 and Colossians 1:20. These two passages describe the reconciling work of Christ on a cosmic scale. In Ephesians, Christ reconciles Jews and Gentiles separated by enmity, uniting them into one body through His cross. In Colossians, the apostle broadens the vision: Christ reconciles not only humanity but "all" — all of creation — by bringing everything back to God. Both passages emphasize the decisive, total nature of the work accomplished by Christ alone.
G0604.portee: This word reminds us that the work of Christ is not a mere forgiveness of sins, but a complete and radical reconciliation: it restores peace with God, unites into one body those who were enemies, and encompasses the restoration of all creation. For the believer, it is an assurance: peace is not fragile or partial, but definitively established by the sacrifice of Christ. It also calls for a life of reconciliation towards others, reflecting the radical work of Christ.

sens: The act of putting something back in place or in condition after an interruption or destruction
The complete renewal of all things at the end of times
G0605.detail:
1. Restoration refers to the action of putting in order, restoring what was damaged or disturbed. The image comes from a construction or an object being placed back in its original position. In Acts 3:21, Peter speaks of the time when heaven must "receive" Christ until the times of the restoration of all things: this is the great renewal that God announced through His prophets.
2. In its biblical usage, the word specifically refers to the final and universal restoration of the created order on the day of judgment. It is the fulfillment of what the prophets have predicted: when God will restore all creation under His perfect authority, putting back in place what sin has disturbed.
G0605.origine: The Greek word is composed of three parts: "apo" (from, since), "kata" (according to, in) and "stasis" (position, state). Literally, it means "putting in position from a starting point." It is the action noun of the verb "apokathistêmi" (to restore, to restore). The central idea is that of a return to a correct position, a putting in order.
G0605.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 3:21. Peter uses it in a speech to the inhabitants of Jerusalem to announce the divine plan of universal restoration. The context shows that this restoration concerns all things and will fulfill what God has announced through His Old Testament prophets. It is an eschatological term, meaning it speaks of the end times and God's final plan.
G0605.portee: This word reminds the believer that God's plan is not only personal or spiritual: it is cosmic. Everything that sin has destroyed or disturbed will one day be put in order. It is a great source of hope: the difficulties and disorders of the world are not final. God has a plan for complete restoration, and the believer can rejoice in this coming renewal.

sens: To be set aside, kept safe
To be held for a future moment
To be destined for someone (figurative sense)
To be destined to necessarily happen
G0606.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: something is kept aside, protected. The servant in the parable "kept" the mina in a cloth (Luke 19:20) — he set it aside, protected it, but did not use it.
2. In a more abstract sense, what is "reserved" awaits its time. Christian hope is "reserved in heaven" (Colossians 1:5): it truly exists, it is secure, but it awaits us up there, for the day we will receive it.
3. Figuratively, being reserved for someone means being destined for them. The crown of righteousness is "reserved" for the faithful servant — it awaits him, it belongs to him in promise (2 Timothy 4:8).
4. Finally, "to be reserved" for humans means to be assigned, inevitable. Death "is reserved" for all men once (Hebrews 9:27): it is a certain and unchangeable fate.
G0606.origine: The word combines the prefix "apo" (away, aside) and "keimai" (to lie down, to be placed). The image is that of something set apart, put in reserve. In Hebrew, it often translates "shiloah" (Genesis 49:10), which refers to what is to come, what approaches, and "chashakh" (Job 38:23), which means what is withheld, hidden. The Greek word brings the idea of something intentionally set aside in waiting.
G0606.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the New Testament. In Luke 19:20, it describes a concrete act: the mina kept, protected. Elsewhere (Colossians 1:5, 2 Timothy 4:8, Hebrews 9:27), it carries a spiritual and often eschatological sense: what awaits us in heaven (hope, the crown), or what awaits humanity (death and judgment). In each case, the emphasis is on certainty and expectation: what is reserved will not disappear, and it will come at its time.
G0606.portee: This word reminds the believer that his promises are not in vain or forgotten: they are "reserved" for him, securely kept in heaven. This invites present faithfulness, knowing that a certain reward awaits him. It also speaks of God's unchangeable order — death, judgment — reminding that everything has a place and a time in His plan.

sens: To cut off someone's head
To take life in a violent and shameful manner
To deprive someone of what is most precious to them
G0607.detail:
1. To behead means to cut off a person's head, usually violently. The Greek word combines "apo" (away, separation) and "kephalé" (head): it literally describes the action of separating the head from the body. This is what Herod orders to be done to John the Baptist: "he sent and beheaded John in the prison" (Matthew 14:10).
2. This verb evokes a brutal execution, an infamous death. When Herod says, "I had John beheaded" (Luke 9:9), he acknowledges this violent act he commanded, which will remain etched in his memory and even trouble his conscience: he wonders if John resurrected has not come back to haunt him (Mark 6:16).
3. Figuratively, it means to deprive someone of what they hold most important: their life, their dignity, their authority. John the Baptist, the forerunner of Christ, loses his head — but not his convictions, as he dies faithful to his preaching.
G0607.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek and literally means "to remove the head": "apo" (away) + "kephalé" (head). It is a compound verb that describes the precise physical action. It appears only in Greek, as it is the language of the New Testament and Greco-Roman antiquity where this form of execution was known.
G0607.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Gospel, always for the execution of John the Baptist: Matthew 14:10, Mark 6:16 and 27, and Luke 9:9. Each account places it in a different context: Herod's order (Matthew), the execution itself (Mark 6:27), and Herod's guilty reflection wondering if John has not resurrected (Luke, Mark 6:16). The term is used only for this grave historical event in the Gospels, never in a figurative sense: it is a verb of history rather than of teaching.
G0607.portee: The beheading of John the Baptist is a turning point in the Gospel: it shows the price of faithful testimony in the face of corrupt political power. John pays with his life for denouncing Herod's wrongdoings. This account invites the reader to meditate on the cost of faithfulness to God and the courage required for preaching repentance, even before the great ones of this world.

sens: To close a door, to shut it
To refuse access, to exclude
G0608.detail:
1. To close a door, to shut it tightly. The word evokes the physical action of closing an access. In Luke 13:25, the master of the house "closes" the door: it is a barrier that closes, an access that is cut off.
2. To refuse access, to exclude someone. The image of the closed door becomes figuratively a refusal to enter, an exclusion. In the same verse, this closed door means that those outside can no longer enter: the master does not recognize those who knock and rejects them.
G0608.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "apo" ("from", "away") and the verb "kleiô" ("to close"). The basic idea is therefore "to close by pushing away" or "to close definitively". The Greek word often translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew verb "sâgar", which means to close, to shut, and also to retain, to imprison. This initial preposition reinforces the meaning: not only do you close, but you close in a way that distances, that keeps away.
G0608.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 13:25. Jesus tells a parable where he speaks of the final judgment: the master of a house closes his door. This eschatological context gives the verb all its spiritual significance. The word describes the moment when the opportunity for salvation closes definitively, when God refuses access to His kingdom to those who have not recognized and followed Him.
G0608.portee: This verb confronts us with the reality of judgment and final exclusion. The closed door reminds us that access to salvation is not eternally open: there is a time to respond to Christ's call, and that time is not unlimited. This should motivate us not to delay the Gospel, but to enter through the door while it is still open.

sens: To slice off a part of the body or an object with a sharp instrument
To remove, to sever, to separate
Figuratively: to exclude, to reject from the community
G0609.detail:
1. The most concrete and direct meaning: to cut, to slice cleanly. Jesus says: "If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off" (Mark 9:43), speaking of radical sacrifices to avoid sin. Peter cuts off the ear of the high priest's servant during Jesus' arrest (John 18:10). The soldiers cut the ropes of the lifeboat to let it fall (Acts 27:32).
2. To sever means to separate or remove something or someone from a group they were part of. It is the same act of cutting, but viewed from the perspective of what is taken away or deprived.
3. In a figurative or moral sense, to be severed means to be excluded, rejected from the community of believers. Paul uses the word this way in Galatians 5:12: "Let those who trouble you be cut off!" — it is a spiritual or ecclesial exclusion, not a physical mutilation.
G0609.origine: The Greek word is composed of "apo" (away, distance) and "koptô" (to cut, to strike), painting the image of a separation by cutting. The root "koptô" evokes the action of striking or trimming, thus cutting off cleanly. The Greek translators of the Old Testament use it to translate Hebrew verbs meaning "to cut" or "to sever" (קָצַץ and כָּרַת notably).
G0609.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament, always with the force of a radical and irreversible action. In Mark, Jesus uses it three times to urge the uprooting of evil (Mark 9:43, 9:45, and implicitly in the context). John uses it for Peter's violent act: cutting off the ear (John 18:10, 18:26). Acts applies it to physical ropes (Acts 27:32). Finally, Paul seizes it in Galatians 5:12 to speak of exclusion from the body of the Church, playing on the versatility of the word: those who sow division deserve to be cut off. The word thus carries both a physical meaning and a spiritual resonance of amputation or rejection.
G0609.portee: This word invites the believer to take seriously the gravity of sin. Jesus does not ask for literal self-mutilation, but a radical and regretless break with what distances us from God — even if it means accepting an apparent loss of ourselves. It is also a warning: remaining in the people of God requires not introducing divisions and scandals. The verb reminds us that belonging to the Christian community is never automatically granted, but calls for faithfulness and moral clarity.

sens: A judgment, an official decision rendered by authority
A response, a verdict
A death sentence
G0610.detail:
1. The word specifically designates a judicial decision rendered with authority, like a judgment or an official ruling pronounced by a court or competent authority. In 2 Corinthians 1:9, Paul speaks of a "sentence" of death: he refers to the death sentence that he and his companions believed they had received.
2. It can also simply mean a response or a verdict, something decisive that addresses a situation or a question. It is the sentence rendered in light of the circumstances.
3. Applied to death, it designates the capital punishment, the definitive sentence that weighs on a life: Paul saw himself as a condemned man awaiting execution.
G0610.origine: The word comes from the verb "apo-krino" (to respond, to judge), composed of "apo" (away, from) and "krino" (to judge, to decide). It literally designates what is "judged and decided" — a definitive response from an authority. The root evokes the image of a judge pronouncing his verdict solemnly and irrevocably. It is a common judicial term in the Greco-Roman world for official decisions and rescripts.
G0610.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Corinthians 1:9, where Paul uses it in the sense of a death sentence. Paul recounts that he and his companions "regarded as certain [their] death sentence." He used a precise judicial term to express the extremity of their situation: they believed they were condemned, awaiting execution. This is not a fictitious judgment, but an inner certainty — a sentence that weighed on them as an inevitable reality. The usage emphasizes the gravity and apparent fatality of their distress.
G0610.portee: This word reminds Christians in distress that God is not bound by the "sentences" that crush us. Paul, faced with what he believed to be his last day, learned to no longer rely on himself, but on God alone, who raises the dead. For us, it is a lesson on divine power in the face of any condemnation — as inevitable as it may seem, God can overturn the sentence and give new life.

sens: To give an answer to someone, to say something in return
To take the floor, to start speaking in a conversation
To express oneself in the face of an accusation or a question (in a legal sense)
To react or act in return to something
G0611.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to give a direct answer to someone: to respond to a question, a reproach, a call. Jesus asks the Apostles, "Who do you say that I am?" and Peter "will respond" (Matthew 16:15-16) by giving his reaction to this question.
2. Often, "to respond" simply means "to take the floor" or "to start saying something," even without a preceding question. John "took" the floor (it is the same word) to recount what he had seen (Luke 9:49), without necessarily having been asked a question first.
3. In a context of judgment or interrogation, the word designates the reaction to an accusation or an official question: Jesus "responded" to the Sanhedrin when he was questioned about his identity (Matthew 26:62-63).
4. More broadly, "to respond" can express an action in return: God "responds" by acting when one prays or calls upon Him (John 5:17, where the Father "acts" in return).
G0611.origine: The Greek word comes from a prefix meaning "from" or "in return" (apo-) combined with a root designating the action of judging, cutting, or separating. The image is one of giving a judgment in return, a separation or distinction in response to what is asked. In classical Greek, it meant "to separate" or "to choose," but in the Bible, it translates the Hebrew "ענה" (anah), which literally means "to lift the voice" or "to speak," and particularly "to respond." The shift from an idea of separation to that of response shows how words transform over time: to respond is in some way to "distinguish oneself" by speaking.
G0611.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the New Testament (245 times), particularly in the Gospels. It appears mostly in Matthew and Mark to report the words of Jesus or his disciples in reaction to questions, accusations, or situations. John also regularly uses it when Jesus "responded" to his interlocutors. Sometimes the word simply means "said" or "took the floor": John "took" the floor to report an observation (Luke 9:49). In other cases, it retains the meaning of "responding" to a question or an accusation: Jesus "responded" to the Sadducees who were trying to trap him (Mark 12:28), or to the Sanhedrin who was questioning him (Matthew 26:62). The word is also used more broadly: Jesus "will respond" at the final judgment by revealing the hidden deeds of men (Matthew 25:45).
G0611.portee: Understanding this word helps grasp the constant dialogue between Jesus and his interlocutors in the Gospels: he does not remain silent in the face of attacks, questions, or the needs of people, but speaks up to teach, correct, or encourage. It is also a call for the Christian: to be able to respond (that is, to account and speak wisely) to those who ask for a reason for the hope that is in him, and to recognize that God Himself "responds" when invoked.

sens: What is said in response to a question or an address
A statement that satisfies the questioner, showing intelligence or wisdom
The refusal to respond, the silence kept in the face of a question
G0612.detail:
1. A response is what one says when someone asks you a question or addresses you. In Luke 2:47, the temple teachers are struck by the intelligence and responses of the young Jesus — he knows what to say in response to their questions.
2. A response can be remarkable for its wisdom or skill: it shows understanding and judgment. In Luke 20:26, Jesus' response to the Pharisees about the tax is so clever that his opponents, "astonished," cannot refute it.
3. Paradoxically, refusing to respond is also giving a response — a response through silence. In John 19:9, when Pilate asks Jesus, "Where are you from?", Jesus does not give him an answer: his silence is itself a form of response.
G0612.origine: The word comes from the verb ἀποκρίνομαι (apokrinomai, to respond), composed of ἀπό (apo, away from, in return) and κρίνω (krino, to separate, to discern). A response is literally a "word of return" — one speaks in echo to what has been heard. The Greek word often translates the Hebrew דָּבָר (dabar, word), showing that in the Bible, to respond is to utter a word that matters.
G0612.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always in Luke and John. In Luke 2:47, it is used in the plural to praise the intelligence of the young Jesus' responses. In Luke 20:26, a single response is enough to disarm the opponents. In John 1:22, the messengers from the Sanhedrin ask John the Baptist for a response about his own identity. In John 19:9, Jesus' silence before Pilate shows that "not responding" is also a form of response. The word always describes a moment when someone speaks or refuses to speak in the face of a serious question.
G0612.portee: This word teaches us that a response is not just a simple mechanical echo: it reveals the wisdom, judgment, and even the dignity of the one who responds. Jesus' responses in the Gospel are never trivial — they contain a word that discerns and liberates. Sometimes, as in John 19:9, silence is the strongest response: he refuses to justify himself before one who does not have the authority to judge the truth.

sens: To conceal something by putting it out of sight
To keep secret, not to reveal
To keep hidden for a time before revealing
G0613.detail:
1. To hide primarily means to put something in a safe place or out of the sight of others. It is the idea of physical concealment or simply removing from view.

2. In a more figurative sense, it means to keep secret, not to let be known. In Luke 10:21, Jesus says that the Father has "hidden" his wisdom from the wise and the learned but has revealed it to children: the Father has intentionally withheld this knowledge from some and given it to others.

3. The richest meaning appears in 1 Corinthians 2:7, Ephesians 3:9, and Colossians 1:26: it refers to a divine secret that God had kept hidden throughout the ages, waiting for the moment it would be revealed. God has not only hidden his mystery, he has "destined it for our glory" (1 Corinthians 2:7) and has now "revealed it to his saints" (Colossians 1:26).
G0613.origine: The Greek word is composed of "apo" (away, out of) and "kruptō" (to hide, to conceal). The latter root refers to the image of something being withdrawn, closed off. The Hebrew "satar" (to hide, to conceal) often expresses the same idea. The prefix "apo" intensifies the action: to hide completely, to set aside.
G0613.emploi: The verb is infrequent (four occurrences), and its uses all show the meaning of keeping secret or hidden. In Luke 10:21, it describes the action of the Father who hides his wisdom from a few. But especially, in 1 Corinthians, Ephesians, and Colossians, the word carries major theological significance: it speaks of the divine "mystery," this plan of salvation through Christ that God had kept secret throughout the Jewish generations, and which apostolic preaching now reveals to the nations. These three epistles use the same language: a long-hidden mystery is now manifested.
G0613.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate an aspect of God's design: long before the world was created, God had a hidden plan, destined for our glory, and this plan concerned Christ and salvation. The Gospel we preach is not an improvisation of God, but the fulfillment of a project he kept secret for ages. This gives depth to our faith: we did not come to faith by chance, but according to an ancient and gracious plan of God.

sens: That which is concealed, kept out of sight
That which is secret, that one wants to keep unknown
That which remains obscure or unknown
G0614.detail:
1. The word designates what is physically or deliberately removed from view: something hidden, kept away from the eyes. In Mark 4:22, Jesus speaks of that which is "nothing hidden" — he refers to secrets or things kept in darkness.
2. By extension, it refers to what is kept secret, what one wants to keep unknown or known only to a few. The word emphasizes the intention to hide, not to reveal. In Luke 8:17, "nothing secret that will not be known": Jesus asserts that secrets do not escape God and will one day be manifested.
3. The word can also qualify what is hidden in a figurative sense: what remains unknown or mysterious until it is revealed. In Colossians 2:3, it is in Christ that "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" — that is, these treasures are securely and mysteriously deposited in him, waiting to be discovered through the knowledge of Christ.
G0614.origine: The word comes from the verb "to hide" combined with the preposition "apart" or "away": it is properly "to hide away, to keep aside." It expresses the action of removing something from sight or knowledge. The family of the word in Greek includes other terms expressing the idea of occultation or secrecy.
G0614.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in important sayings or explanations. Jesus uses it in his teaching through parables: in Mark 4:22 and Luke 8:17, he asserts that what is hidden will be revealed — a promise that nothing escapes God's judgment and that the truth will soon manifest. In Colossians 2:3, Paul applies it to the mysterious divine wisdom hidden in Christ: what is mysteriously hidden in Christ is, however, accessible to the believer who knows him. The meaning remains constant: what is removed from view or knowledge, awaiting revelation.
G0614.portee: This word invites the believer to remember that God sees all that is hidden: no sin, no escaped thought remains secret before him. It gives both a salutary fear and a confidence: for one who hides in guilt, revelation is daunting; for the believer who asks Christ for the hidden wisdom in him, it is a promise of access to God's treasures.

sens: to take life, to cause physical death
to execute judicially
to seek to kill, to desire someone's death
to destroy, to annihilate
to kill spiritually, to take away the life of the soul
G0615.detail:
1. To kill means to take someone's life. This is the most direct meaning: the Jews asked Pilate for "permission to put someone to death" (John 18:31). Jesus warns his disciples: do not fear those who "kill the body" (Matthew 10:28).
2. To execute by judgment or official decree. When they "put Jesus to death" (Matthew 26:4), it refers to a legal condemnation. "The Jews who killed the Lord Jesus" (1 Thessalonians 2:15): this is the judicial act of the authorities.
3. To seek to kill, to pursue someone with the intention of causing their demise. "The Jews sought to kill him" (John 5:18): the hostile intent is clear, even if the murder has not yet been accomplished.
4. To destroy, to completely annihilate. In Revelation, the plagues "kill" a third of mankind (Revelation 9:18): this is massive destruction. "Death reigns" and "kills" (Revelation 6:8).
5. To kill spiritually, to take away divine life. "Sin produced death in me" (Romans 7:11): sin kills the soul by separating it from God. "The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life" (2 Corinthians 3:6): legal observance without grace kills the soul.
G0615.origine: The word comes from the Greek prefix "apo" (away, distant) and a root meaning "to strike" or "to kill." It is a compound word that reinforces the idea of destruction: not just to strike, but to strike to take life, to annihilate. In Hebrew, the verb often used for "to kill" is "harag" (הָרַג), which appears as early as the story of Cain and Abel. The Greek word also translates the verb "mut" (מוּת), "to die," when used in the causative: to cause to die.
G0615.emploi: This verb appears 71 times in the New Testament. It is very frequent in the Gospels, especially in Matthew and John, to describe threats against Jesus and his disciples. The religious authorities seek to "kill" Jesus (John 5:18, John 7:1). It is also used for persecutions against the disciples: "They will deliver you to death" (Matthew 10:21). In Revelation, the word refers to divine plagues that "kill" entire peoples (Revelation 6:8, Revelation 9:15, Revelation 9:18). The verb also takes on a figurative meaning: sin "kills" man (Romans 7:11), the Law "kills" spiritually (2 Corinthians 3:6). This richness shows that "to kill" is never neutral in the Bible: it is always a serious act that separates from good and from God.
G0615.portee: This word reminds us of the gravity of death and the price of life. It also shows that Jesus intentionally faced hostility and death for us. When we read that sin "kills" or that the Law without grace "kills," we understand that our salvation comes through the cross of Christ, who has annihilated the power of death. It is a call to grasp that only God gives true and eternal life.

sens: to deliver, to give birth to a child
to produce something that comes forth as a fruit
to bring to completion, to carry a reality to its conclusion
G0616.detail:
1. To give birth in the strict sense: it means to bring a child into the world, to carry a pregnancy to term until delivery. This is the medical sense of the word, which designates the act of birth itself.
2. To produce in a figurative sense: just as a mother gives birth to a child, one can say that an immaterial reality "gives birth" to something that comes forth. In James 1:15, sin is the child produced by desire (lust). The word emphasizes what is born in a living and autonomous way, not just as a mechanical consequence.
3. To bring to completion or to its conclusion: the word ἀποκυέω implies that the birth results in — that the child comes into the world healthy and alive. Similarly, when the text says "He brought us forth according to his will" (James 1:18), it means that God has brought us to our complete and current existence, deliberately and effectively.
G0616.origine: The word comes from two parts: ἀπό ("from, out of") and κυέω or κύω ("to be pregnant, to bear"). The addition of ἀπό gives the idea of completion, of an action that goes all the way: not only the pregnancy, but the actual giving birth. It is the precise medical term for birth, which gives it a connotation of accomplishment and reality in common language.
G0616.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in James. In James 1:15, it describes how desire (lust) "gives birth" to sin as a mother gives birth to her child — which shows that sin is born from an inner matrix and develops until its completion (death). In James 1:18, God is the one who "gives birth" to us according to his will, by his word of truth, which emphasizes that our existence as Christians is born from a voluntary and living act of creation on God's part. The word suggests each time not just a simple causation, but a living generation that leads to being.
G0616.portee: This word shows that sin is not an abstraction that falls upon us from the outside: it is born from within us, like a child from its mother. This holds the believer accountable — our desire carries within it the seed of sin. Conversely, the fact that God has "given birth" to us reminds us that our identity as Christians does not come from us, but from a creative act of God. We are his creations, begotten by his will and his word.

sens: to roll a stone or an object from one place to another
to remove or take away by rolling
(Figuratively) to remove the obstacle that prevents access to something
G0617.detail:
1. The concrete meaning is simply to roll something, like a stone that is pushed to roll: it is the physical action of rolling movement. In Genesis 29:3 and 10, the shepherds rolled a large stone to remove it from the well in order to water the flocks.
2. In the context of the resurrection, the verb takes on the meaning of removing or taking away by rolling: in Matthew 28:2, the angel rolls the stone away from the tomb entrance. The women in Mark 16:3 wonder who will roll the stone for them, as it was very large and blocked access to the sepulcher.
3. Beyond the physical action, this gesture symbolizes the removal of the obstacle: the rolled stone is the obstacle removed, which allows access to the tomb and the discovery of the resurrection.
G0617.origine: The word comes from the Greek root κυλίω (kuliō) which means "to roll." The prefix ἀπό- (apo) means "away from" or "aside": the complete word thus means "to roll away." This root evokes the image of a round object moving by turning on itself. The Hebrew גָּלַל (galal) translated in the Septuagint by this same verb carries the same notion of rolling a stone.
G0617.emploi: The verb appears 4 times in the New Testament, only in the resurrection accounts (Matthew 28:2, Mark 16:3-4, Luke 24:2). In Matthew 28:2, it is the angel who rolls the stone from the sepulcher. In Mark 16:3, the women worry about who will roll the stone, as it was very large; verse 4 specifies that they discover the stone has been rolled away. In Luke 24:2, the women find the stone rolled away from the tomb. The verb is always used to denote the removal of the stone from the sepulcher, and it emphasizes each time the miracle of the resurrection: what seemed impossible to the women (the stone was too large) has been accomplished.
G0617.portee: This verb reminds the reader of a central truth: Christ is risen, and the stone that sealed his tomb could not stop him. For the believer, this act of rolling away the stone speaks of the divine power that abolishes obstacles, including death itself. It is an invitation to see that nothing can prevent what God accomplishes.

sens: to obtain something from another person
to receive in return what one has given
to take someone aside, to separate them
to obtain what is due, the reward or punishment
G0618.detail:
1. This verb primarily means to receive something that someone else gives or hands over to you. It is the act of taking what is offered to you: in Luke 18:30, the one who has left family and home to follow Jesus "will receive much more in this age." 
2. It can also mean to receive in exchange, that is, to obtain in return what one has given. When one lends to someone to "receive back" (Luke 6:34), one expects to be repaid. This is the principle of give-and-take. 
3. In Mark 7:33, the verb means "to take aside" or "to separate": Jesus "took him aside from the crowd." This reflects the image of the prefix "apo" (away, apart): one receives or takes someone by setting them apart. 
4. The word also denotes receiving what one deserves: the punishment or reward that is rightfully due to us. In Luke 23:41, the wrongdoer acknowledges: we "receive what we deserve for our crimes." In Colossians 3:24, the slave "will receive from the Lord the inheritance as a reward" — he will obtain what is due to him.
G0618.origine: The verb is composed of the prefix "apo" (away, from) and the verb "lambanô" (to take, to receive). The basic image is thus "to receive from someone" or "to take for oneself" what comes from elsewhere. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament often translates the word "laqah" (to take, to receive) with this verb, especially when it involves receiving something in exchange or in return. The prefix "apo" reinforces the idea that one receives something distinct, from the outside.
G0618.emploi: This verb appears about ten times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospel of Luke and the letters of Paul. It is used to receive material goods, rewards, or punishments. In Luke 16:25, Abraham tells the rich man: you "have received your good things during your lifetime" — he obtained his earthly pleasures. In Romans 1:27 and Galatians 4:5, it refers to receiving what is due: retribution or redemption. In Colossians 3:24 and 2 John 1:8, the word denotes the heavenly reward that God grants. Sometimes (Mark 7:33, Luke 15:27), the meaning shifts from "to receive" to "to take aside" or "to find again," but the idea of receiving or obtaining remains central. The nuance varies according to the context: receiving passively (help, grace), receiving actively (taking), or receiving in exchange (payment, punishment).
G0618.portee: This verb reminds us that everything a Christian possesses — their goods, their life, their faith — comes from God and is entrusted to them. It also indicates that God does not give service for service: when we serve God or love without expecting a human return, we "receive" from God Himself the true reward, far beyond what we hoped for (Luke 18:30). It is an invitation not to live as a calculator of earthly exchanges, but in trust that God sees and rewards.

sens: Pleasure or satisfaction derived from the use of something
Delight derived from a possession or experience
Consciously enjoying a good that is offered
G0619.detail:
1. Enjoyment is primarily the concrete pleasure one feels in using something: it is truly tasting a good, deriving contentment from it. When Paul advises the rich "to put their hope in God, who richly provides us with everything for our enjoyment" (1 Timothy 6:17), he speaks of this ability to receive with gratitude and appreciate the goods that God offers — food, health, friendships. 
2. By extension, enjoyment becomes the broader pleasure derived from a situation or state: it is the well-being of a condition, the comfort of life. But in Hebrews 11:25, Moses refuses "for a time the enjoyment of sin" — not that he is unaware of the momentary pleasure that sin can provide, but he rejects it because it is better to suffer with the people of God than to indulge in that fleeting satisfaction.
G0619.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "apolauô" (to enjoy, to benefit from), composed of "apo" (from, starting from) and "laudô" (to take). This image of the verb — "to take from" — suggests a conscious, voluntary action: it is not a pleasure that imposes itself against one's will, but one that is willingly taken and allowed. The word thus expresses an act: to receive and welcome a good.
G0619.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Timothy 6:17, Paul speaks of the enjoyment of material goods that God gives us — they must be received with gratitude and used without pride. In Hebrews 11:25, the author contrasts the fleeting enjoyment of sin with the glorious suffering of remaining faithful to God: the pleasure of sin exists, but it is temporary and not worth the path of faith. Each time, the word touches on a choice: what do I truly choose to taste? Which pleasures are worth savoring?
G0619.portee: This word reminds Christians that receiving God's goods — whether material or spiritual — is not shameful, provided it is done with gratitude and without idolatry. But it also invites them to discern: there is an enjoyment that sin promises, alluring and brief, and a deep joy that comes from remaining faithful to God, even at the cost of suffering. Choosing true enjoyment means learning to appreciate good things according to their true value.

sens: To leave something or someone in a place, to depart and abandon it there
To abandon, renounce someone or something
To reserve, keep on hold for future use
G0620.detail:
1. To leave something or someone in a place means to physically depart while leaving it where it is. This is the most concrete meaning of the word. For example, Paul says, "I left the cloak that I had at Troas with Carpus" (2 Timothy 4:13), or "I left Trophimus sick at Miletus" (2 Timothy 4:20) — these are simply things or people he has departed from, leaving them behind. This is also the meaning when Paul says, "I left you in Crete" (Titus 1:5), meaning he entrusted Titus with a responsibility as he departed.
2. To abandon or repudiate someone means to leave them voluntarily, often definitively or with a break. In Matthew 5:32 and Luke 16:18, the word refers to the man who "repudiates his wife" — he dismisses her, sends her away, breaks the marriage. This is a more serious and voluntary abandonment than simply "to leave."
3. To be reserved or remain on hold means to be kept for future use or entry. In Hebrews 4:6 and 4:9, it speaks of what is "reserved" — what remains available, set aside for the one who will need it. This is a passive nuance of the word: what is not yet used, but kept in reserve.
G0620.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "apo" (which means "away from, apart") and "leipo" (to leave). The basic image is that of departing, moving away while leaving something behind. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this Greek word often translates "yathar," which means to leave, set aside, or leave intact. The composition of the word ("apo" + "leipo") emphasizes the idea of abandonment or separation: one does not simply leave, one goes far away.
G0620.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, primarily in the epistles and the epistle to the Hebrews. In Paul, it denotes the action of leaving something or someone in a place (2 Timothy 4:13, 4:20; Titus 1:5): it is a practical verb describing concrete gestures or decisions. In the words of Jesus reported by Matthew and Luke, the word takes on the meaning of "repudiating" the wife — it is a legal or marital use of the verb "to leave." In Hebrews 4:6, 4:9, and 10:26, it appears in the passive voice and means what is "reserved" or "remains" available, emphasizing what is kept on hold rather than the action of abandoning. In Jude 1:6, it describes the angels who "abandoned" their own dwelling — a radical and culpable abandonment.
G0620.portee: This word helps the reader understand that "to leave" can signify very different realities: simply leaving a place, abandoning a responsibility or a person, or keeping in reserve for future use. For the Christian, Hebrews 4:6-9 reminds that God's rest is reserved — offered and available — to the one who believes, showing that the divine promise remains always active and accessible. In Jesus' words about marriage (Matthew 5:32; Luke 16:18), the word "repudiate" reveals the seriousness of divorce in God's eyes: it is not a simple "to leave," but an abandonment that violates the marriage covenant.

sens: To pass the tongue over something
To eat, devour eagerly (especially for an animal)
G0621.detail:
1. To lick means to pass the tongue over a surface: it is the natural gesture of an animal licking a wound or food (Luke 16:21, where the dogs lick the sores of poor Lazarus).
2. In context, the image becomes one of eager and degraded consumption: Lazarus, reduced to misery, longs to be fed with the crumbs that fall from the rich man's table, and even the dogs of the house come to lick his wounds — that is, without respect for his human dignity. The verb emphasizes the total humiliation of one whom no one cares for or helps.
G0621.origine: The Greek word is formed from the prefix "apo-" (which means "from," "down") and the verb "leichô" (to lick). This composition reinforces the idea: it is not just simple licking, but an act that strips or consumes. The base verb "leichô" is common for describing the gesture of animals, and the initial preposition gives it a shade of insistence or repetition.
G0621.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 16:21, in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus. Jesus describes the extreme misery of the beggar lying at the rich man's gate: not only is he hungry and sick, but he suffers the indignity of seeing the dogs lick his sores. This is the final detail of progressive humiliation: Lazarus is so abandoned that even the animals that come to touch him highlight his lack of protection and dignity. The moral context of the parable emphasizes the contrast between the carefree wealth of the first and the total distress of the second.
G0621.portee: This raw image of human degradation challenges the reader regarding responsibility toward the poor and suffering. Jesus does not describe misery to find beauty in it, but to awaken conscience: to ignore the one who suffers at our door is to refuse to see Christ himself. The verb "to lick" reduces human dignity to nothing, inviting the disciple never to allow others to be reduced to a state of worthless creature.

sens: Completely annihilate, destroy, kill
Lose something permanently
Be annihilated, disappear, cease to exist
Perish, die, be in danger
Be spiritually lost, separated from God
Wander astray, like a sheep that strays from the shepherd
G0622.detail:
1. To completely destroy something, reducing it to nothing: Herod seeks the child "to make him perish" (Matthew 2:13), or Jesus says, "the thief comes only to steal, kill, and destroy" the sheep (John 10:10). This is the action of annihilating what exists.
2. To lose something one possessed and no longer find it: an old wineskin can "be lost" if new wine is put into it (Luke 5:37), or Jesus says, "whoever loses his life for my sake will find it" (Matthew 10:39) — this is renouncing something voluntarily or involuntarily.
3. To be destroyed, disappear, cease to exist: the garments of Christ will age "and will be changed; but you remain, and they will perish" (Hebrews 1:11) — this is the passive destruction of what was.
4. To perish, die physically or be in mortal danger: the disciples cry, "Lord, save us, we are perishing!" in the storm (Matthew 8:25) — this is the immediate feeling that one is going to die or be destroyed.
5. To be spiritually lost, that is, separated from God and destined for condemnation: "the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost" (Luke 19:10), or "whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not believe in the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:16 implicitly).
6. To stray, turn away from the right path, like the image of the shepherd and the lost sheep (Matthew 15:24) — this is to drift away, to lose sight, no longer being safe with the one who is supposed to protect you.
G0622.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ἀπό (apo-, "away from") and ὄλλυμι (ollumai, "to destroy"), which conveys the idea of destroying by distancing or completely separating. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates אָבַד (avad), which also means "to perish, to be lost, to disappear." This root ἀπ- also produces other verbs of separation and destruction (ἀποθνῄσκω, "to die"). The original image is that of an irreparable rupture: something goes far away and does not return, or ceases to exist.
G0622.emploi: The verb appears 87 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). In the active voice, it means "to destroy, to kill" (Herod wants to "perish" the child Jesus, Matthew 2:13; the thief comes to "destroy" the sheep, John 10:10). In the middle or passive voice, it means "to perish, to be lost, to disappear" (the disciples "perish" in the storm, Matthew 8:25; the garments of Christ "will perish," Hebrews 1:11). The meaning enriches spiritually: to be "lost" is to be separated from God (the "lost sheep of Israel," Matthew 10:6; the tax collector Zacchaeus was "lost," Luke 19:10), and it is the central word to describe eternal condemnation (those who "perish," 1 Corinthians 1:18; "whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not believe in the Son shall not see life," John 3:16). Nuance: sometimes it is a temporal loss (the wineskin that is lost, Luke 5:37; the crumbs that the disciples gather so that nothing is "lost," John 6:12).
G0622.portee: This word reveals to the Christian reader two decisive truths: first, that there is a real, spiritual, and eternal perdition — it is not an abstraction, but a definitive separation from God. Secondly, that Jesus came precisely to seek and save "what was lost" (Luke 19:10), so that faith in him pulls us from the condition of "lost" and places us in that of "saved." This verb calls each one to examine whether they are lost without Jesus or found in him.

sens: The angel of destruction of the king of the locusts from the abyss
G0623.detail: 1. Apollyon is the Greek name of the angel who reigns over the creatures of the abyss (Revelation 9:11). It is a title that literally means "the Destroyer," formed from the verb "to destroy." John tells us that this celestial being also has a name in Hebrew: Abaddon, which has the same meaning. In the vision of Revelation, he appears as the king of the monstrous locusts that rise from the abyss to torment men.
G0623.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb ἀπολλύω (apolluô), which means "to destroy, to lose, to annihilate." It is formed from the prefix ἀπό (apo, "from, away from") and the verb λύω (luô, "to loose, to dissolve"). The image is that of what disintegrates, breaks apart, destroys. In Hebrew, Abaddon comes from the root ָאבַד (abad, "to perish"), which carries the same idea: this name describes the essence of this celestial character, his nature as a destroyer.
G0623.emploi: The word Apollyon appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 9:11. John mentions it in his vision of the fifth trumpet, when the locusts from the abyss torment men for five months. The apostle specifies the name of the king who commands them, first in Hebrew (Abaddon), then in Greek (Apollyon), so that his Hellenic readers understand exactly who reigns over these infernal creatures.
G0623.portee: For the Christian, Apollyon embodies the destructive opposition to the will of God. Seeing this Greek name and its Hebrew equivalent side by side emphasizes that the destruction of God's enemy is immutable, inscribed in all languages and cultures. It reminds us that Satan is never more than what he is: a destroyer, an adversary without ultimate power, subject to divine sovereignty that even sets the limits of his action.

sens: City of Macedonia in ancient Greece
G0624.detail: Apollonia is a coastal city in Macedonia (region of northern ancient Greece), located on the road between Amphipolis and Thessalonica. Paul and Silas passed through it during their second missionary journey, as reported in Acts 17:1.
G0624.origine: The name Apollonia comes from Apollo, the Greek god of the sun and the arts. Several cities in the Mediterranean bore this name, all founded in honor of this god. The city mentioned in Acts is probably the Macedonian city located on the coast of the Aegean Sea.
G0624.emploi: Apollonia is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:1. Paul and Silas pass through it during their evangelistic journey through Macedonia, traveling from the coast inland to reach Thessalonica, the large city where there was a Jewish synagogue. This city serves as a simple geographical stop in the narrative of the Gospel's progression into Europe.

sens: Preacher and Jewish teacher of the 1st century
Jew from Alexandria
Eloquent man well-versed in the Scriptures
Collaborator of Paul in the early Church
G0625.detail: 1. Apollos is an important figure in the early Church, a Jew from Alexandria known for his eloquence and deep knowledge of the Scriptures (Acts 18:24). He is a powerful preacher who arrives in Ephesus and actively engages in the ministry of the Word. 2. Originating from the great city of Alexandria in Egypt, Apollos brings the scholarship and Hellenistic Jewish culture characteristic of this community (Acts 18:24). 3. His gift of eloquence makes him a captivating speaker for the churches, particularly in Corinth where some become his disciples to the point of forming a faction around his name (1 Corinthians 1:12). 4. Although admired for his charisma, Apollos remains a servant of the Lord just like Paul: one plants, another waters, but it is God who gives the increase (1 Corinthians 3:5-6). This complementary relationship shows that the different gifts of biblical leaders do not make them competitors but workers of the same master.
G0625.origine: The name Ἀπολλῶς is probably a shortened form of the Greek name Ἀπολλώνιος (Apollonius), itself derived from the Greek god Apollo. The diminutive suggests familiarity with Greek culture. It is a common name in the Mediterranean world of the 1st century, particularly among Hellenized Jews living in the diaspora.
G0625.emploi: Apollos appears ten times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and Pauline correspondence. He is first introduced in Ephesus as an eloquent teacher with an incomplete knowledge of baptism (Acts 18:24-19:1): he had only known the baptism of John. His ministry quickly develops in Corinth, where the community divides into factions, some preferring him over Paul or Peter (1 Corinthians 1:12, 3:4). Paul uses the image of Apollos watering what Paul has planted to show the unity of evangelical workers despite their differences (1 Corinthians 3:6). His oratorical talents are recognized but contextualized in a perspective of humility: like Paul, he is a servant, not a master. He is also mentioned as a probable defender of the faith in 1 Corinthians 16:12 and recommended in Titus 3:13.
G0625.portee: Apollos shows that eloquence and personal talent, while valuable, must remain at the service of Christ and His Church, never the foundation of division or rivalry among believers. His example invites honoring different gifts without absolutizing them and reminds that the true worker of the kingdom remains a humble servant. The mention of his incomplete baptism and his discreet correction by Aquila and Priscilla encourages disciples to continually grow in the knowledge of God.

sens: Respond to an accusation or criticism by presenting arguments or explanations
Speak in one's own favor before a court or authority
Justify one's action or thought in the face of objections
Express oneself or speak in order to clarify one's position
G0626.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the action of responding to an accusation by giving one's reasons. When Paul "made his defense" before Governor Felix, he sought to refute the charges against him by explaining his innocence (Acts 25:8).

2. It is also used for the act of speaking in favor of one's cause before a judge or authority. Before King Agrippa, Paul requests permission "to speak for his defense" (Acts 26:1), that is, to plead his case.

3. The word can also mean "justify," in the sense of showing the righteousness of one's conduct or thought. When Paul writes to the Corinthians that he "justifies himself" before them, he intends to clarify his intentions and ministry in light of criticism (2 Corinthians 12:19).

4. Sometimes it simply denotes the act of speaking or taking the floor in a context where an explanation is expected. Alexander, pushed by the crowd, "wanted to speak to the people" to, no doubt, explain himself (Acts 19:33).
G0626.origine: The word comes from two parts: "apo" (from, starting from) and "logos" (word, speech). It literally means "to speak from oneself" or "to express oneself for oneself." The image evokes someone who takes the floor to expose their position and clarify misunderstandings. In classical Greek, it is a judicial term: one who defends themselves responds to accusations. The term "apology" in French comes directly from this Greek root.
G0626.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Acts and in Paul. It mainly describes scenes of defense before authorities: Paul defends himself before Felix (Acts 24:10, 25:8), Festus (Acts 25:8), King Agrippa (Acts 26:1-2, 26:24). It takes on a theological dimension in Paul: before the critical Corinthians, he "justifies himself" to clarify his apostleship (2 Corinthians 12:19). Romans 2:15 uses it in a more general sense: the conscience of the Gentiles "defends" them when it accuses them, meaning it speaks in favor of or against their actions. Jesus also uses it: He invites His disciples not to prepare their defense in advance before courts (Luke 12:11, 21:14), for the Spirit will inspire their words.
G0626.portee: This word speaks to the Christian confronted with hostility or misunderstanding: it shows that accounting for one's faith and actions is legitimate and necessary. But Jesus' teaching nuances its use: the disciple should not be anxious in crafting their defense; they can rely on the Spirit. It is an invitation to trust in God and to be sincere, rather than anxious or cunning. Paul's example also demonstrates that an honest and courageous defense of faith is a form of testimony.

sens: Speech or argument to refute an accusation
Action of justifying oneself before one's accusers
Fact of proving one's innocence or good faith
G0627.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a speech delivered to refute an accusation made against oneself. It is a judicial plea, like that of Paul before Governor Festus (Acts 25:16) or the one he requests to make before the crowd in Jerusalem (Acts 22:1).
2. More broadly, it signifies the action of justifying oneself, proving one's innocence or good faith in the face of reproaches. Paul states that his accusations are like his "defense" before the Corinthians (1 Corinthians 9:3): he does not deny the facts, he explains them.
3. The word can also refer to the entire effort to confirm the truth one defends: Paul speaks of the "defense and confirmation of the Gospel" (Philippians 1:7), so that "defense" then approaches the meaning of "justification" or "vindication."
G0627.origine: The word comes from the verb « ἀπολογέομαι » (apologia, literally "to speak away from"), composed of « ἀπό » (apo, "away from") and « λόγος » (logos, "word"). The starting image is that of speaking away from, or against, accusations — one defends oneself by speaking. It is a legal and assembly term, common in classical Greece to designate a plea.
G0627.emploi: The word appears seven times in the New Testament, mainly in Pauline epistles and in Acts. Paul uses it in a judicial context (his defenses before Roman authorities: Acts 22:1; 25:16; 2 Timothy 4:16) and in a pastoral or missionary context (his justification before the churches: 1 Corinthians 9:3; Philippians 1:7). In 2 Corinthians 7:11, it takes on the meaning of moral "justification": the Corinthians have shown their purity. The context varies, but the central idea remains: it is always a response to an accusation or doubt.
G0627.portee: This word reminds the Christian that they may have to account for their faith and conduct — before authorities (like Paul), before the Church, or before those who question them. But it also shows that legitimate defense does not consist of denying or fleeing: it is to speak clearly and honestly. For the modern reader, it is an invitation to cultivate honesty and openness, and to be ready to explain their faith without fear (1 Peter 3:15).

sens: To be physically cleaned by removing a stain
To be purified from guilt or a moral blemish
To be transformed by renouncing a sinful past
G0628.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, it means to remove a stain, dirt: the verb describes the action of washing to become clean. This is the idea of physical cleaning, as in the Old Testament where one rinses with water (Job 9:30).

2. In a figurative sense, it means to morally purify oneself from guilt or sin. In Acts 22:16, Paul tells the new convert: "Be baptized, and be washed from your sins" — baptism symbolizes here the erasure of faults, as if the water carries away the stain of sin.

3. More broadly, it means to be transformed and redeemed: in 1 Corinthians 6:11, "you were washed" means that the converts have broken with their past of sin through Christ. It signifies the transition from a defiled life to a purified and new life.
G0628.origine: The verb comes from the root *louō* (to wash) preceded by the prefix *apo* (to remove, take away). The image is that of water removing a stain: in washing, one gets rid of what dirties. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates Hebrew words like *rakhats* which evoke ritual cleaning or ablution. The family of the verb includes words for bath and cleaning, all centered on the idea of purification.
G0628.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament. In Acts 22:16, Paul encourages a new believer to be baptized to be "washed from his sins" — baptism is presented as a sign of divine forgiveness and breaking with the past. In 1 Corinthians 6:11, Paul reminds the Corinthians that they "were washed" and sanctified: he contrasts their former dissolute life (they practiced immorality, theft) with their current state of purity through Christ. In these two passages, the verb is used in the passive or middle voice, emphasizing what has been done *for* the believer, not what he does himself.
G0628.portee: This word reveals that Christ truly removes the guilt and sin of the believer, just as water removes dirt. It is the assurance that one can leave behind a life of evil and start anew in Christ. Baptism is the visible sign of this, but the reality is internal: it is the power of the Holy Spirit that transforms, that "washes" the one who believes.

sens: Liberation obtained by the payment of a ransom
Deliverance from sin and its consequences through the work of Christ
Future liberation of the body and all creation at the return of Christ
Fulfillment of the adoption of the children of God
G0629.detail:
1. The word first evokes the concrete image of a prisoner or slave being freed by paying a ransom for him (Hebrews 11:35 speaks of women who refused this deliverance, preferring resurrection). It is a costly purchase that grants freedom.
2. In the New Testament, this concrete sense becomes a figure of salvation: Christ paid the price for our liberation from sin with His shed blood. Romans 3:24 says that we are "freely justified by His grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus" — meaning that Christ accomplished what we could not do ourselves.
3. Redemption extends to the body and the future: Romans 8:23 speaks of the expectation of "the redemption of our body," when our entire existence will be transformed and freed from corruption (1 Corinthians 1:30).
4. It also encompasses the completion of our adoption as children of God: Ephesians 1:14 presents redemption as the crowning of our inheritance, what God guarantees us and that we will receive fully.
G0629.origine: The Greek word comes from "apolutroō" (to free in exchange for a ransom), itself composed of "apo" (away, from) and "lutron" (ransom, price of liberation). The root "luo" means "to unbind, to free." In Hebrew from the Old Testament, the word "goel" (redeemer) and its derivatives (like "peduyim", the redeemed) express the idea of a relative or protector who pays to free a family member from slavery or ruin.
G0629.emploi: The term appears 10 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Paul speaks of it mostly in connection with justification (Romans 3:24) and the future transformation of body and soul (Romans 8:23). In the Epistles to the Ephesians and Colossians, redemption is linked to the blood of Christ shed for us (Ephesians 1:7, Colossians 1:14) and to our inheritance in God (Ephesians 1:14). Hebrews 9:15 speaks of the new covenant of which Christ is the mediator, bringing eternal redemption. Luke 21:28 uses the word more for future and imminent deliverance — the time when Christians will see the end times approaching.
G0629.portee: This word reminds us that our salvation is a costly purchase, which God paid for with the death of His Son. It frees us from guilt, from the slavery of sin and death, but also opens up the hope of complete transformation of our being — body, soul, and spirit. Redemption does not stop at conversion: it continues until the day we are fully renewed and live in the presence of God.

sens: To free someone from captivity or detention
To send away, dismiss, let go
To break the bond of marriage through divorce
To forgive, absolve from faults
To let go, allow to depart
G0630G.detail:
1. To free someone who is held, imprisoned, or in custody: it means breaking their chains or bonds. Pilate asks the crowd if he should release Jesus or Barabbas (Matthew 27:17), meaning to let him go free instead of condemning him to death. It also conveys the idea of the master forgiving the debt of his servant and releasing him from prison (Matthew 18:27).

2. To send someone away, dismiss them, ask them to leave. Jesus tells the disciples: "Send the crowd away" (Matthew 14:15), meaning let them go find food elsewhere. After healing a man, Jesus sent him away (Luke 14:4). It is an act of authority and kindness: the one who releases decides to let the other go.

3. To break the marriage bond through divorce, meaning to release one's wife as a wife. Matthew 1:19 and 5:31 speak of releasing (i.e., divorcing) the woman, which was a known practice. Jesus takes up this usage and questions its meaning.

4. To forgive offenses, as one would release someone from their debt to you. Jesus says: "Forgive, and you will be forgiven" (Luke 6:37), meaning forgive and you will be pardoned. It is an image of moral and spiritual liberation.

5. To let go, authorize departure, often after the person has been held or could have been kept. The brothers let Paul and Silas return (Acts 15:33), they did not want to hold them back.
G0630G.origine: The word is composed of "apo" (away, distance) and "luo" (to unbind, detach). It literally means "unbind away from," "separate by unbinding." The root "luo" evokes the action of undoing a knot or bonds, hence the idea of liberation and separation. The Greek word translates the Hebrew "shoub" (to return) and other terms of liberation. It is a term from legal and administrative vocabulary: to free a prisoner, to send away a crowd, to pronounce a divorce.
G0630G.emploi: This verb appears 51 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. It is very frequent in the Passion narrative: Pilate considers several times releasing Jesus (Matthew 27:17, Mark 15:9, John 19:10), which shows that it was his right as governor. In the Gospels, Jesus releases or sends away the sick or crowds (Luke 14:4, Matthew 14:15). The word is also used for divorce (Matthew 5:31-32, Mark 10:2, 4, 11-12), a subject to which Jesus returns and redirects towards the permanence of marriage. In Acts, it designates the departure authorized by the authorities (Acts 3:13, 15:33) or the release of the apostles after their arrest (Acts 4:21, 5:40). The meaning nuances according to the context: strict liberation, administrative dismissal, breaking of bonds, or spiritual forgiveness.
G0630G.portee: This word shows us that human freedom (of movement, conscience, bonds) is important and that it is never absolute: it depends on the one who has authority. More profoundly, it speaks of forgiveness as a liberation: to release someone is to set them free from their guilt. For the disciple, it is a call to release others from their offenses, just as God has released us through Christ. It is also a call to refuse retention and vengeance, and to prefer mercy.

sens: Remove dirt or a stain by pouring water or immersing in water
To distance oneself, reject
To purify or exonerate oneself morally
G0633.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of washing by pouring or rubbing with water to remove a stain. In Matthew 27:24, Pilate washes his hands: this concrete gesture signifies that he uses water to remove any trace of guilt, as if washing his hands could erase his responsibility.

2. The word can also express the rejection or distancing of something: to wash one's hands of someone means to dissociate from them, to push them away.

3. On a moral and religious level, washing represents spiritual purification or an attempt to exonerate oneself before God or men. Pilate literally washes his hands to symbolically indicate that he is washing himself of the guilt of Christ's blood — a gesture meant to declare his innocence before the crowd, even though water can never truly erase that responsibility.
G0633.origine: The word is composed of apo ("to distance from") and niptō ("to wash"). The root niptō comes from an ancient Greek family denoting the action of washing, particularly hands or feet. In Matthew and Mark, this verb is mainly used for ritual ablutions: Jesus criticizes the Pharisees who wash their hands before eating according to tradition. The Old Testament uses Hebrew verbs like shataph ("to inundate") or rakhaç ("to wash") for ritual or physical purifications.
G0633.emploi: The verb appears only once in Matthew 27:24, at the crucial moment of Jesus' trial. Pilate, confronted with the pressure of the crowd demanding crucifixion, performs a symbolic gesture: he washes his hands in front of witnesses. This moment is laden with irony: the Roman governor intends to purify himself through this rite, as the Jews practiced, but this washing of hands — an external gesture — cannot erase the decision he makes to send an innocent man to death. The context places this verb at the tragic turning point of Jesus' judgment.
G0633.portee: This passage reveals how one might believe they can justify themselves through an external gesture, even a religious or solemn one, while guilt resides in the heart and in the decision. For the believer, it serves as a reminder that God cannot be deceived by appearances or empty rituals: only true repentance and a new covenant in Christ truly purify. This moment also illustrates the impotence of human power before the will of God.

sens: To detach and fall from a place where one was attached
To suddenly disappear, to vanish
G0634.detail:
